thread.title: Trump-Xi Meeting: The China Trade Deal Wall Street Needs

author: JED GRAHAM
title: Trump-Xi Meeting: The China Trade Deal Wall Street Needs
text:
Wall Street isn't looking for peace, love and understanding out of President Donald Trump's Saturday dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping. But the stock market will be in for a negative surprise if the Trump-Xi meeting ends with signals that the planned U.S. escalation of tariffs will go forward.
X A China trade war truce is probably too much to ask for at this point. The best that can be hoped for is the status quo, with a signal from the U.S. that the 10% tariffs on $200 billion in Chinese imports won't jump to 25% on Jan. 1, as they're set to do. Trump has also hinted at further China trade war escalation, by imposing tariffs on all Chinese imports.
The two leaders "had been scheduled for a 90-minute one-on-one meeting followed by dinner," but the Trump-Xi meeting was essentially downgraded, wrote UBS chief U.S. economist Seth Carpenter earlier in the week. "Having a working dinner without a side meeting reduces the likelihood of full resolution of the dispute between the two countries."
A halt to the escalating China trade war would fuel optimism that the U.S. and China can hammer out a deal in the months ahead.

Please contact customer service CLOSE Trump-Xi Meeting: 'Positive Tone' "We expect a positive message and tone" to emerge from the G20 meeting, along with a framework for moving ahead with U.S.-China trade talks, Carpenter wrote.
Yet he also sees "risks the trade talks could fall apart." UBS says its optimism has ebbed lately due to recent U.S. statements and actions. Those include a recent "scathing" Trump administration report on Chinese intellectual property practices; a "hard-line tone" taken by Vice President Mike Pence at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit; additional tariffs announced on Chinese aluminum; and movement to expand the set of technology goods subject to export restrictions to China.
If there is no deal, and Trump tariffs remain set to escalate, expect the Dow Jones industrial average to take a hit. After Trump talked of hitting Apple ( AAPL ) with 10% tariffs on the iPhone , Apple stock may be among the losers.
Predicting the outcome of U.S.-China trade talks is difficult, with actions by both Trump and Xi sometimes hard to interpret. Yet the case for a positive outcome is pretty strong.
U.S.-China Trade Deal Fell Apart In May First of all, the sides were pretty close to a deal in May, when China reportedly offered to buy $70 billion worth of American goods over a couple of years to modestly narrow the U.S. trade deficit. At the time, President Trump crowed about the tentative China trade deal being a big win for American farmers. Instead, China has essentially stopped buying U.S. soybeans.
Now that Trump has played his tariffs card, credibly threatening tariffs on the full half-trillion in Chinese imports, he would surely much rather bring home a somewhat better China trade deal than come up empty-handed. Having lost the House in the midterm elections, with weak results in some key Midwest states, Trump could feel more pressure to produce something positive.
The stakes were further raised earlier this week, when General Motors ( GM ) announced it would close U.S. plants in Ohio and Michigan in a restructuring.
On top of that, Daimler ( DDAIF ) and BMW have discussed moving manufacturing of American-made SUVs that are bound for China. Beijing retaliated against Trump tariffs with an additional 25% tariff on auto imports from the U.S. That puts tariffs on U.S.-built cars at 40% vs. 15% for cars made in Europe.
Trump, Xi May Seek 'Tactical' Trade Deal If Beijing sweetens its offer, Trump might be willing to jump at it. After all, he'd still be able to take on Chinese trade practices at the World Trade Organization and move ahead with plans to restrict technology exports.
Meanwhile, the Chinese economy has slowed under pressure from Trump tariffs. China's Xi Jinping is too proud to bow to Trump, but he should be willing to offer a deal that doesn't impede China's global economic ambitions.
In other words, a China trade deal might resolve near-term problems for Trump and Xi, but underlying U.S.-China tensions are likely to keep building.
"Any agreement in Argentina will be a tactical pause at best, providing short-term relief to jittery stock markets and beleaguered U.S. farmers, but having no material or long-lasting effect on the slide toward a high-stakes geopolitical competition between the United States and China," explained Ely Ratner in Foreign Affairs.
